clue.text: Express's leader article about twice-married luvvie

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of the newspaper name is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of Express

indicators.note: 'about' asks for the article and the married pair to be turned round, read from the far end

parts.note: the indefinite article
M is the abbreviation for married, written twice

explanation.surface: A tabloid's editorial dishes the dirt on an actor with two weddings behind them.
explanation.walkthrough: A luvvie is British slang for a theatrical actor, here Emma Thompson or a similar thespian; the article and the two Ms are turned round after E.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma Thompson is a well-known British stage and film actress, the sort the press mockingly calls a luvvie.

clue.text: Share a single bed and have a big laugh!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to share sleeping space meant for one
second meaning: to bend over helplessly with laughter

explanation.surface: Two people squeeze into one narrow bed and find the whole thing hilarious.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both sharing quarters or a bed and bending over in convulsions of mirth.

clue.text: Stupid management relied on by many a TV presenter?

definitions.text: relied on by many a TV presenter?

parts.note: a stupid person is an idiot
a company's management is its board

explanation.surface: A dim television executive team props up the people who appear on screen.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also hints at a dig at TV bosses, but the definition is the prop itself.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiot board is the cue card held beside the camera so a presenter can read their lines.

clue.text: (see 10ac.)
(see 10ac.)
Screw, having changed top? That's gross!

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word for screw is swapped for a different one

parts.note: a vulgar synonym for having sex

explanation.surface: A crude remark about sex that turns into a cry of disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue does not say what the new top letter is; the definition 'That's gross!' points to Y in place of the F.
explanation.definitionFit: Yuck is the exclamation people make when they find something disgusting or revolting.

clue.text: She usually does/doesn't have plenty up top

definitions.text: She usually does/doesn't have plenty up top

parts.words: She usually does/doesn't have plenty up top
parts.note: surface reading: a woman described by the size of her chest
setter's reading: plenty up top in the bust, but not much up top in the brain

explanation.surface: A sniggering description of a busty woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up top' has two senses: the bust, which she has plenty of, and the head, which she does not.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a derogatory label for an attractive woman stereotyped as having little intelligence.

clue.text: It takes live piss-artist to get infatuated

definitions.note: besot means to make infatuated, so the clue's phrase is loose

parts.note: to be is to live or exist
piss-artist is British slang for a drunkard, and a sot is a drunk

explanation.surface: Only a living drunk could fall so hopelessly in love.
explanation.definitionFit: To besot is to turn someone foolishly infatuated, so being besotted is being smitten.

clue.text: Emulates Lord Lucan — bestial females answer: "Bed!"

parts.note: does are female deer, rabbits and the like
A is the abbreviation for answer
a bunk is a narrow bed

explanation.surface: A lurid tale of animals and bedding attached to a notorious peer.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Lucan was a British earl who vanished in 1974 after his children's nanny was murdered, and was never found.
explanation.definitionFit: To do a bunk is British slang for running off or disappearing, as Lucan famously did.

clue.text: A couple of shots did for him? Not if it was Charles!

definitions.text: A couple of shots did for him? Not if it was Charles!

parts.words: A couple of shots did for him?
parts.note: surface reading: a man killed by gunfire, as a famous US president was
setter's reading: shots of whisky, of which two would hardly trouble a politician known for his drinking

explanation.surface: A grim joke about an assassination swerving into a jibe at a politician's drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: John F Kennedy was shot dead; Charles Kennedy, then Liberal Democrat leader, was known to drink heavily, so 'shots' flips from bullets to drams.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to the assassinated US president and to the British party leader with a drink problem.

clue.text: (& 5/4) Rev. Blair's mouthpiece spins a lot, brainwashes — devious Alastair's head must go!

indicators.note: devious means crooked and roundabout, so the letters are bent out of their order
the first letter of the named man is to be dropped from the mix

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
the first letter of Alastair, to be removed

explanation.surface: A jab at Blair's spin machine and his press chief Alastair Campbell.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one A from SPINS A LOT BRAINWASHES and rearrange. Private Eye ran St Albion's Parish News as a spoof parish newsletter from the Vicar, Rev. Tony Blair.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eye's long-running spoof cast Blair as a trendy vicar, with this parish newsletter as his voice to the flock.

clue.text: To enter more firmly is accepted as part of group relations

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to write over pencil in permanent ink

definitions.text: accepted as part of group relations
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read as two words: inside the family circle

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the phrase into 'in' plus 'kin', being among one's relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: Inking in confirms a pencilled booking or answer permanently; being in among kin means belonging to the family.

clue.text: Auntie Beth rudely secretes the buzzer

indicators.note: to secrete is to hide away, so the name conceals the next piece inside itself

parts.note: the name rearranged

indicators.note: done rudely, the name is roughly handled and its letters knocked about

parts.note: a bee is an insect that buzzes

explanation.surface: An aunt called Beth is caught hiding a buzzing gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: Auntie (or Auntie Beeb) is the affectionate British nickname for the BBC; 'Auntie Beth' looks like one name but splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nicknames are familiar British names for the BBC, the national public broadcaster.

clue.text: Forced evacuation has bearing on name change

indicators.note: a change of order lets the letters of the word for a label be rearranged

parts.note: a compass bearing, east
the word rearranged

explanation.surface: Sounds like a bureaucratic note about an emergency evacuation and a rebranding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forced evacuation' suggests people fleeing a building; here it is the bowels.
explanation.definitionFit: An enema flushes liquid into the rectum to make the bowels empty, a deliberately induced clear-out.

clue.text: The tale about Linford Christie?

indicators.note: 'about' here means turned around and moved about, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is telling a story concerning a famous runner.
explanation.walkthrough: Linford Christie is a British sprinter, Olympic 100m champion in 1992; the question mark flags him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Christie is one instance of a sportsman who competes in track events, hence an example of the general term.

clue.text: Perhaps Brenda's attendant "makes one decide to get screwed by a lot of Mounties"

indicators.note: only a good part of the police force's initials is used, not all of them

parts.note: one is A, joined to the verb and rearranged

indicators.note: something screwed up is twisted out of shape, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
the Mounties are the Royal Canadian Mounted Police

explanation.surface: A mock tabloid quote about a royal servant and a troop of Canadian police.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-standing nickname for the Queen. Drop RC from RCMP to leave MP.
explanation.definitionFit: An aide-de-camp is an officer serving as personal assistant to a senior figure, and the monarch has several.

clue.text: (& 24) Drugs and shagging followed by tart for a Dagenham piper, perhaps?

parts.note: E is ecstasy, so Es are the pills
shagging is British slang for having sex
tart is old slang for a young woman

explanation.surface: A party-girl lifestyle linked to a famous troupe of bagpipers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dagenham Girl Pipers are a bagpipe band from Dagenham, in Essex; the Essex girl is a British stereotype of a brash, party-loving young woman, which the wordplay plays up.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl piper from Dagenham, a town in Essex, would literally be a young woman from that county.

clue.text: (& 17/18) Offensively inferior bloke swallowing ecstasy ordered Stan to be gobbled by Prince

indicators.note: the name is put in a new order, its letters rearranged

parts.note: a chap is a man
E is the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: a mouth swallowing something takes it inside, so the man's word wraps round the drug
being gobbled up means ending inside, so the jumbled name goes within the royal's name

parts.note: Prince Andrew, informally Andy
the name rearranged

explanation.surface: A sleazy tale of a man on pills and a royal with an appetite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince' is Prince Andrew, Andy to the tabloids.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something both poor in quality and unpleasant, shoddy as well as tawdry.

clue.text: Old haunt of sailors requiring intercourse on thigh

parts.note: intercourse in its old sense of conversation
the ham is the back of the thigh

explanation.surface: Randy sailors in port looking for a bit of how's-your-father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intercourse' is the sexual sense in the surface but social talk in the wordplay. Chatham in Kent was a Royal Navy dockyard town until 1984.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kent town housed a major naval dockyard for centuries, so seamen were based and roistered there.

clue.text: (see 16ac.)
(see 16ac.)
Having sniffed, Cyclops has to go down pretty sharp

parts.note: to nose is to sniff around
the setter speaking, I've, means I have

explanation.surface: The setter admits to a sniff of something and a rapid comedown.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the setter, so 'Cyclops has' is the setter saying I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosedive is a steep plunge, so to nosedive is to fall or drop very sharply.

clue.text: One returning to stuff Heath, got changed

definitions.note: adapted alone means changed; 'got' pads the phrase

parts.note: A as one

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the word for stuff is read from its end

parts.note: to pad is to stuff with filling
Ted Heath was British Conservative prime minister 1970-74

explanation.surface: A former prime minister has his wardrobe sorted out.
explanation.definitionFit: To adapt something is to alter or modify it for a new use, so adapted means modified.

clue.text: My organ's sexy look

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the magazine Cyclops sets for, Private Eye, nicknamed this
second meaning: to give someone a come-hither glance

explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' suggests something rude, but it is a publication, the setter's own magazine; it is also literally a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Eye calls itself by this short name, and the phrase also means a flirtatious, inviting glance.

clue.text: Not engendered, you might say, when it's in action

indicators.note: 'in' places the first item inside the word for action

parts.note: a deed is an act
'it' is old slang for sex appeal or sex

explanation.surface: Something about lacking gender, oddly said to occur during the act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not engendered' is a punning way of saying 'with gender removed', hence the 'you might say'.
explanation.definitionFit: To desex is to neuter or remove sexual characteristics, playfully read as being stripped of gender.

clue.text: Red Peril, debut of George Bush's no.3, is trash

indicators.note: a colour put in peril is thrown into disorder, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the colour rearranged

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so the first letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of George

indicators.note: number three points to the third letter of the surname

parts.note: third letter of Bush

explanation.surface: A Cold War jibe about communism and a US president's deputies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red Peril' reads like 'the Red Menace', the Cold War fear of communism.
explanation.definitionFit: Dregs are the worthless residue left at the bottom, figuratively the rubbish or lowest part of something.

clue.text: Hot and woozy, very lacking Conservative front-bencher

indicators.note: lacking means without, so the abbreviation for very is taken away

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
woozy means hazy or vague

explanation.surface: A senior Tory looking flushed and fuzzy-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: V is the abbreviation for very. William Hague was a former Conservative leader, then on the front bench.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hague sat on the Conservative front bench as a senior shadow minister after leading the party.

clue.text: (see 15dn.)
Arsehole in dire need has church going downhill morally

indicators.note: dire means in a terrible state, so the following word is wrecked and rearranged
'in' places the rogue inside the scrambled word that follows

parts.note: the word rearranged
an arsehole, in British slang, is a contemptible man, a cad
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A desperate scoundrel watches the church slide into sin.
explanation.definitionFit: Decadence is moral decline or deterioration, a slide into self-indulgence and decay.

clue.text: Bust comes to a point — dandy!

parts.note: a bust, a failure, is a dud
a point of the compass, east

explanation.surface: A cleavage that ends in a point, apparently.
explanation.definitionFit: Dude originally meant a fastidious, fashionable man, a fop, before its casual American sense.

clue.text: "Oaten's end brought by craft" — informant

indicators.note: end points to the final letter of the surname

parts.note: last letter of Oaten
Noah's ark is a craft, a vessel

explanation.surface: A quoted tip-off about a politician's downfall and a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Oaten was a Liberal Democrat MP brought down by a sex scandal in 2006. A nark is British slang for a police informer.
explanation.definitionFit: A nark is slang for a police spy or someone who informs on others.

clue.text: Suicide bomber's aim: to blow up right mad Tory Malcolm's butt

indicators.note: something blown up is scattered, so the following letters land in a new order

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: a butt is the end of something, so the last letter of the name is taken

parts.note: last letter of Malcolm

explanation.surface: A terrorist plot targeting a deranged Conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tory is probably Malcolm Rifkind, but only his last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Such attackers seek death for their cause, believing it makes them a martyr, so that is their goal.

clue.text: Little woman with runs has American illness

parts.note: Vi is the short form of the woman's name Violet
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
US for American

explanation.surface: A small woman with diarrhoea has caught a bug from the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The runs' suggests diarrhoea, fitting the illness picture, but it is just the cricket abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A virus is an infectious agent, and the word is commonly used for the illness it causes, a bug.
